Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00273

In the first sense, food must be a particular physical substance. It must be a substance, because an accident cannot become a substance or part of one. It must be physical, because what is immaterial cannot turn into a body. And it must be particular, because a universal body does not exist in the external world. So the food of every body is a particular physical substance. We observe that animals do not feed on simple bodies but only on compounds, since a simple body is too unlike them, while a compound is more like them. Plants do not disprove this, as some suppose.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00274

The truth calls for a different kind of explanation, one that goes beyond the level of discussion people are used to. Here is a hint. Anything that exists in its own right, whether a natural thing or a soul, is one existing being. Yet one being may contain the capacities for several different things. Its activity, too, has one source while it can take several forms.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00275

Every plant or animal body is one existing thing. The elements are present in it as capacities, not as separately existing elements. So, in our view, nourishment does not mean that a body called “food” enters the body it nourishes to replace what has worn away. Nor does growth mean that the body’s size increases because more external matter is added to it. Rather, suitable moist matter next to a plant or animal prepares the soul’s power to flow into the body, preserving its size or bringing it to the degree of growth needed at each moment. As we explained earlier, the body’s change in size is a continuous flow of magnitude from an active power into receptive matter.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00276

If nourishment meant that a foreign body entered the nourished body, the body would not remain one individual at every moment. Likewise, if growth meant that the quantity added were greater than what was lost, there would not be one individual subject undergoing growth. The same applies to decline. The truth is as we have indicated.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00277

You must also understand that the way food completes the body it nourishes is like the way knowledge completes a learner, or an idea that is actually understood completes a mind that could understand it but has not yet done so. Something may be capable of being known before it is actually perceived or understood. What completes a sense is something actually sensed, such as an image present in the sense—not colors, sounds, tastes, or smells as they exist in external matter. In the same way, what completes the intellect is something actually understood: an intelligible form present in an intellect that understands it, not an external thing such as a heavenly sphere, an animal, a plant, or the earth.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00278

We have shown by proof that things actually sensed are joined in their being with the perceiving subject, and that things actually understood must likewise be joined in their being with the intellect. What completes a thing is identical with what it completes: the perceiver is what it perceives, and the knower is what it knows. Likewise, the nourished body and its food become one when the food has actually become part of that body, not when it is merely capable of nourishing it. Wheat, for example, has only a remote potential to nourish. the partially digested fluid formed from it in the stomach is closer to becoming food; the material formed in the liver is closer still; and blood in the veins is closer to being food than all these earlier stages. What reaches an organ and becomes flesh, bone, or another organ is food in actuality—and it is that very organ being nourished.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00279

Food and the body it nourishes are one and the same existing thing once nourishment has taken place. They differ only when the mind analyses the process: it may consider the body or organ on its own, before the new completion reaches it, or consider it as complete, with the perfection it has gained through the earlier actions and changes that prepared it. This is like the way the soul is completed by acquiring forms of knowledge. One of the subtle points that can bring insight here is that the stages of digestion correspond to the stages of abstraction in understanding.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00280
IV. The Four Stages of Digestion
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00281

Know that animals, and human beings too, need food as long as they remain in this world and have a bodily nature. Their food must resemble the body it nourishes, in both form and matter, because these bodies are constantly changing and wearing away. Each organ needs its own share of food, suited to it and like it. The body's nutritive power matures and transforms the food, then strips away its husks and waste. This power stands to the body as the intellect stands to the soul.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00282

When food enters the body and comes under the soul's nutritive power, that power works on it through subordinate powers. It changes the food through stages of digestion, using their natural craft like alchemy to make it pure—free of adulteration, waste, and husk. Digestion and transformation take place in four stages. The first is in the stomach, though it begins in the mouth. We know this because chewed wheat can bring boils and abscesses to a head in a way that wheat boiled in water cannot. The first digestion is complete when the food reaches the stomach and is cooked by its blazing heat, which, when asked, “Are you full?” replies, “Is there any more?”
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00283

The body's powers, placed in nature's service, purge the food of the sins of its waste. They refine what has strayed from obedience to God and from the balanced unity that is nature's straight path for governing bodies according to divine wisdom. The food becomes like a thick, milky liquid called chyle. The second stage begins when these powers have finished their work in the body's lower region and the chyle rises from that dark place to another: the liver. There, other powers and keepers take over and cook and dissolve it again. Some of its remaining impurities and waste fall away, and it becomes the four humours, partly distinct and partly mixed—“they have mixed a good deed with a bad.”
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00284

Of these four, the best is the substance called blood. Some of it passes along the vessels called mesenteries toward the heart. There it follows the soul's command and undergoes training, exertion, and purification for a time, until it is ready to receive the soul's form. The rest travels through the veins to the organs, where it is digested once more. After its remaining waste is removed, it takes on the likeness of the organs. Each portion of blood becomes like a particular organ, joins it, and is drawn to it, just as the portion fit for the heart is drawn there. Each part is drawn to what resembles it.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00285

The waste products correspond to the four stages of digestion. Waste from the first stage, in the stomach, is excreted as stool through the intestines. Most waste from the second stage leaves as urine through the bladder; the rest is carried off by the spleen and gall bladder. Waste from the third stage leaves in sweat and through other visible openings, such as the nose, ears, and eyes—as tears—or through openings we cannot see, such as the pores. Some waste from the fourth stage leaves as semen. The rest leaves through what grows beyond the body's needs—hair, nails, dirt, and other matter expelled by the body's nature, such as burst abscesses and the like.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00286
V. What the Powers of Nourishment and Growth Really Are
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00287

You have learned from our approach that a definition can explain what a thing is or explain its existence. We have already distinguished these questions. We may explain what a thing is by naming the broader kind it belongs to and what distinguishes it from other members of that kind. But existence itself has no parts, so it cannot be explained in that way. If an existence is complete, it is defined through its agent and its end; if it is incomplete, through its action. As we indicated earlier, the definition of an existence and the proof that it exists are one and the same. A proof that explains why something exists is stronger than one that shows only that it exists.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00288

On this basis, every power is a simple instance of existence, and powers can be identified by what they do. We identify the nutritive power by its effect: it changes food into something like the body it nourishes, replacing what the body has lost. Every power is a source of change in this world. Each change has a form and a material, and each action has an end. Here, the form is food's change into something like the nourished body; the material is the food; and the end is replacing what has worn away. In effect, we have said that the nutritive power performs this action, in this place, for this end.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00289

The growth power, by contrast, is defined as the power that increases a natural body's dimensions, in natural proportion, until it reaches its full growth, by adding to its original parts. “Increasing a body's dimensions” rules out artificial changes: if a craftsperson adds to a candle's length and width, its depth must shrink, and the reverse is also true. “In natural proportion” rules out abnormal swelling, such as dropsy and other tumours. “Until it reaches its full growth” rules out getting fat. And “adding to its original parts” points to the difference between growth and fattening.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00290

A clarification about the real reason for this last difference: growth is a movement in the very substance of the organs, so the power that moves them nourishes and increases their substance. Fattening, however, comes from foreign matter entering the organs and adhering to them. Nourishment and growth each involve three things: first, obtaining food that is potentially like the body being nourished or grown; second, joining it to that body, as is commonly thought; and third, making it actually like the body. If the amount added to the original substance of the organs equals what has worn away, that is the work of the nutritive power. If it is greater, that is the work of the growth power.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00291

At this point, someone may object: nourishment and growth are really one power. The only difference is that the nutritive power adds as much as has worn away, while the growth power adds more. The difference between them is therefore only a matter of greater or lesser strength. If a power is strong enough to do something, it is strong enough to do the same thing again. So if the nutritive power can restore the original part, it should also be able to add another part like it. When this power is especially strong, it should both replace what was lost and add to it. At the start of life, it is strong enough to do both; later, it weakens and replaces only what was lost.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00292

The fact that the nutritive power supplies less than what is lost in old age, but supplied as much as was lost in middle age, seems to support this objection. Its supply is greater in middle age than in old age, so one power may supply different amounts at different times. This is a strong objection.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00293

I answer that different natural ends show that the powers themselves differ. The end of nourishment is to repair what has been lost through bodily change. We see this when an animal does not seek food until hunger's heat has taken hold in the stomach and the body has been depleted. Then it desires food. The end of growth is to extend the organs in particular proportions. Adding more food than the body loses does not always produce growth—or even growth at all. Sometimes the body takes in more food but grows less; at other times, the reverse is true. We often see boys and girls grow rapidly during puberty even while a serious illness has weakened their nutritive power and prevented it from doing its work. So if these two powers sometimes produce opposite results, they must differ in their very nature, not merely in strength. If the difference were only greater or lesser strength, they could differ only in degree. But they can differ in opposite ways: growth may increase while nourishment decreases, or nourishment may increase while growth decreases. They differ in what they do and in what each is for. That establishes our point.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00294

Here is a doubt, and a closer look at it. Some people claim that the nutritive power is fire. They argue: “The nutritive power nourishes, and fire nourishes, so the nutritive power is fire.” Apart from the faulty form of the argument—which draws a conclusion from two affirmative statements in a pattern that does not allow it—the claim that fire nourishes is false. Fire does not nourish; it arises and rises by its nature. Once it rises, cold air takes hold of it and destroys it. There is no single fire that is being nourished. Still, the work of the nutritive power resembles fire's work in maturing and transforming things.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00295

Others say that there are empty spaces in the organs which the growth power fills. This is false, as we have already indicated: filling a gap does not make an organ grow. Nor do we accept the account Avicenna gives in The Healing, and some scholars approve: that the growth power separates the parts of an organ, then food particles enter the gaps between them. The same explanation is also offered for nourishment.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00296

When parts are separated, the result is inherently painful. It is impossible that nature or the soul should carry out a natural action that is inherently at odds with the body it inhabits—one that would cause constant pain if there were a power that sensed it and the sensing were actually taking place. As we have already discussed, separation of parts is inherently painful. A single power cannot cause or require two opposing effects.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00297

The truth, as we have established, is that growth is a continuous movement in quantity. Change means that an ability which has not yet been realized gradually becomes real. Here, the process is gradual because, at every moment, the thing that moves has a different instance of quantity. In growth, there is no fixed amount to which another amount is added, whether by matter entering the organ or by any other means.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00298
VI. Why the Powers of Nourishment and Growth Stop, and Why Death Is Necessary
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00299

First, let us present the arguments people have made on this subject. Then we will set out a general principle from divine metaphysics and philosophy as a whole, which God has taught us and which will clarify this question and others like it.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00300

The usual explanation for why growth stops is this: bodies are formed from blood and semen, so every newborn is moist, as we see in children before birth. Gradually, dryness takes hold. You have learned that growth is thought to happen only when the organs stretch, as food passes through their pores. This is possible only while they remain soft. Once they harden and dry out, growth stops. So growth continues from birth until the organs have hardened and dried; then the growth power stops. That is the usual explanation.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00301

As for why the nutritive power stops and death follows, several arguments have been offered. The first is that the nutritive power is bodily, so its actions must be limited. But this is contradicted by the heavenly souls, which are bodily powers—especially according to Aristotle and his followers, who say that these souls are present in their bodies—yet their actions are supposedly unlimited. Avicenna's reply was that, although they are bodily, the light of a separate intellect shines on them, enabling them to act without limit. His student Bahmanyār wrote to ask: if you allow this, why could bodily powers not also receive the ability to act without limit from that separate intellect? Avicenna answered that this is impossible because the body is made up of opposing elements. From his answer we can see that merely insisting that bodily powers must have limited action does not settle the matter. We must examine what follows from the body being made up of the basic elements. The second argument is this: in The Canon, Avicenna says that after the age when growth stops, the body's natural moisture must keep diminishing until it disappears altogether. Heat gradually consumes this moisture; once it is gone, the body's natural heat must also die out. That is when death occurs.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00302

We say that this moisture must diminish for three reasons. First, the surrounding air acts on it with its heat and dries it out. Second, the body's natural heat helps to dry it from within. Third, the movements of the body and soul add to the effect. Someone may ask: why can the nutritive power not replace the moisture as it wears away? We answer: suppose that in old age this power supplies as much as it did in youth. Even so, more moisture is consumed in old age than in youth. So what the nutritive power supplies is less than what is lost. The body must then keep losing moisture, which leads to decay and death. The older a person becomes, the stronger the effect of these three drying forces: dryness increases, heat decreases, and the nutritive power weakens further. If this continues, it eventually stops altogether, and death follows.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00303

The objector may reply that the amount consumed was once equal to the amount supplied in youth. If supply and loss are no longer equal in old age, either the consuming forces have grown stronger, so that more is consumed, or the nutritive power has weakened, so that it supplies less. The first option is false, since there are only the three causes just mentioned: internal heat, external heat, and bodily and psychic activity. These causes were present in youth just as they are in old age. If the consuming forces have not increased, then the amount consumed cannot have increased either. The second option is also false, since the nutritive power weakens only when heat decreases, and heat decreases only when moisture diminishes. If we then say that the moisture diminishes because the nutritive power has weakened, we reason in a circle, which is impossible.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00304

One might reply that the consuming forces in old age are the same three forces that were present in youth, but they act for longer. A weaker force may have a stronger effect than a stronger one if it acts for longer. So the drying forces may act longer in an old person than in a young one and cause more dryness. This argument has no weight. The nutritive power also works for longer, just as the forces that cause dryness do. If a drying force increases dryness by acting for longer, the nutritive power should likewise increase the body's nourishing moisture by acting for longer.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00305

A view close to this one is attributed to Socrates. He said that the natural heat in semen, once it reaches the womb, acts like the heat of an oven on a loaf that sticks to it. The oven first works on the surface until a kind of crust forms. Then its heat enters through the crust and works the inside into shape until the loaf is cooked. In the same way, the heat in semen first forms a crust. It then spreads through the growing body in proportion to its length, width, and depth. If the body's substance has little moisture, the formative power completes its shape in six months. If it has abundant moisture, the body takes longer to form, sometimes as long as 304 days. A newborn is still dominated by moisture, which is why it cannot stand upright or move about. The natural heat that the Creator has placed within it gradually dries the moisture in its organs. First it becomes ready to sit; then it can move without standing; then it can stand; then it can walk. These differences, too, depend on the gradual loss of moisture, which is why children begin to walk at different ages.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00306

The natural heat continues this work in an animal's body until its moisture is completely used up. The heat then goes out because it has lost what sustained it, and death follows. The cause of death is thus the same as the cause of life. Life would not occur if heat did not prevail over moisture; yet as heat prevails, the moisture is depleted, and when it is gone, the heat also disappears. God has measured out the heat so that it overcomes moisture, first bringing life and later bringing death. This is what is reported in the commentary on The Canon. We have already discussed the weaknesses in this view. It deserves careful attention, though: when examined fully, it proves sound because it leads back to the principle we will establish.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00307

The third argument, found in the works of careful investigators, is this: the cause of death in all animals is that the replacement supplied by the nutritive power, though enough to replace what is lost and even more than enough in quantity, is not enough in quality.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00308

The explanation is that the body's original, innate moisture first matured in the vessels that hold food, then in the vessels that hold semen, and finally in the womb. The replacement supplied by the nutritive power matures only in the first of these, not in the other two. It is therefore not fully mixed or matured, and does not reach the quality of what it replaces. It cannot fully take its place. Its strength is less than that of the original moisture, like replacing oil in a lamp with water. As long as the original quality prevails over the acquired quality in the mixture, natural heat grows stronger and supplies more than is lost, so the mixture grows. But once the second quality appears and weakens the first, the heat stops and can no longer supply more than what is lost.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00309

When the acquired quality prevails, the mixture declines and the heat weakens, until nothing remains of the original quality. Then death necessarily follows. This shows that the original, innate moisture begins to decline in quality from the moment it first forms, and that this is what eventually spoils the mixture. It also shows that even if the nutritive power were unlimited and supplied replacement for what was lost without end—not in a fixed amount, but in proportion to what was lost—the replacement still could not match the original in quality, even if it matched it in quantity.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00310

I say that this argument, too, is weak and persuasive rather than conclusive, for several reasons. First, we do not accept that semen has a stronger and finer temperament than the animal materials formed later. If its temperament were more balanced and finer, the soul's powers would flow into it from the beginning, and it would be alive and able to speak. That is plainly false. Second, the material of semen is not present as separate parts in the animal's body, some with the temperament of semen and others with the temperament of the replacement food, as this argument assumes. So one cannot say that semen's temperament is stronger while the replacement is weaker.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00311

Third, we do not accept that proper maturation and fermentation, or a strong temperament, depend on their having occurred in those particular vessels. A temperament may arise elsewhere and be firmer and stronger than one formed in those vessels. We see this in animals that do not come from parents but arise in other ways; some formed this way have a stronger temperament than those produced by reproduction. So the temperament of the replacement supplied by the nutritive power could be stronger and firmer than the temperament of what is lost. This argument therefore fails to prove that death is necessary.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00312

These are the three arguments people have offered for the necessity of death, along with the objections to them. Avicenna points to all three in the general discussion of The Canon. He says that after growth stops, heat must begin to decrease because the surrounding air draws moisture from its source; the body's natural heat helps from within, and bodily and psychic movement—necessary for life—helps as well. Nature cannot resist this forever, because all bodily powers are limited and therefore cannot keep supplying replacement without end. If this power were unlimited, it could supply what is lost continuously, not in one fixed amount. But loss does not stay constant; it increases day by day. The replacement cannot keep pace, and the loss consumes the moisture. Moreover, another cause helps extinguish the heat: foreign moisture, which keeps arising when digestion fails. It puts the heat out in two ways: it smothers it, and it gives the body a cold, phlegmatic quality. This is natural death.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00313

From “We must understand” through “bodily and psychic movement necessary for life,” Avicenna points to the second argument. From “Nature cannot resist this” through “cannot keep supplying replacement without end,” he points to the first. From “If this power were unlimited” through the end, he points to the third.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00314

The fourth argument is that if individual human beings lived forever, those who came before us would have used up the matter from which we are formed, leaving none for us. Even if matter remained, there would be no room or provision for us. If we and those who come after us remained forever nonexistent while earlier people alone continued to exist, that would go against wisdom: they have no greater claim to eternal existence than we do. Justice requires that everyone have a share in existence. So those who exist first must die, allowing those who come later to exist. This argument, too, is merely persuasive and weak: it does not show that every individual must die.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00315

The fifth argument is that if death were not necessary, an unjust tyrant could remain in the world forever, continuing to do evil and spread corruption, while those he wronged would have no hope of justice. That would surely lead to disorder. This argument is also weak: it does not show that everyone in the world must die. A tyrant's existence may have some purpose. And just as a whole class of tyrants may continue to exist in this world—as we see and know—so may one tyrant or several. The wronged can receive justice in ways other than the tyrant's death.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00316

The sixth argument is that if death and the afterlife were not necessary, the devout and good would be the most miserable of people, since they would have given up worldly pleasures without receiving anything in return. That would encourage people to sin, pursue pleasure, and turn away from everything else, bringing evil and disorder. This argument, like the two before it, treats death in terms of incidental ends. None of these is a primary cause or an essential end. We are looking for an essential cause that can serve as a premise in a proof. It must be either a proximate efficient cause, as in natural philosophy, or an essential end, or a remote efficient cause, as in divine metaphysics. The previous three arguments are neither natural efficient causes of death nor essential final causes. They are only incidental consequences, which cannot serve as the basis of a proof—only of persuasive speech and the like.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00317

These matters follow from death's true end; they are not that end itself. Death's true end is the existence of the everlasting world and the arrival of souls at their own stations, whether levels of happiness or depths of misery. Death does not happen primarily so the earth's matter will remain for those who come later, or so the wronged may take revenge on the tyrant, or so the righteous may be repaid for their pain and hardship in this world. Those are consequences of death's true end.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00318

Now that you have seen the weakness of these arguments, let us offer one that proves the necessity of death. From the standpoint of reason, possible beings are either originated or generated—in another wording, complete or incomplete. An originated being remains, because both the cause that brings it into being and its ultimate goal remain. A generated being, however, must perish. Its complete cause includes motion and time, and every motion must come to an end. When the cause, or even one part of it, ends, the effect must also cease. So everything generated must perish. Animal bodies are plainly generated and continually renewed; they must therefore perish and die.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00319

Complete beings remain because they were not made to serve as matter or as a means for another being. For this reason, each kind of them consists of a single individual. Incomplete beings, by contrast, naturally give rise to another being. They are prepared causes for other beings. If they remained forever, they would not be incomplete but complete—and that is a contradiction.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00320

Understand that death is natural, not because bodies cannot last forever. As you have learned, they may continue through change and an influx from above. Nor is natural death caused by the nutritive power's inability to supply food forever in the right amount or quality; we have already shown the weakness of such claims and others like them. Death is natural because powers and souls are always turning toward, and moving from, one level of existence to another. Divine metaphysics has shown that natural motions and actions have ends.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00321

In our discussion of causes, we proved that the true goal of an action must bring the agent itself to a fuller state of existence. In truth, the end belongs to the agent. An incidental end is a benefit that follows from the true end. For example, sexual desire results in children, and the heavenly powers bring about new beings; these are incidental ends.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00322

The true end of the plant powers is to become food for animals; the true end of animal powers is to provide food and other things for human beings. As for human powers, the body's motive power aims to obtain material for nourishment and growth, while the perceptive power aims to provide material for the intellect or the soul's powers: imagined forms, estimated meanings, and the first principles of reason. Once the human soul has developed the powers that were previously only possibilities—whether toward angelic intellectual happiness or toward satanic, predatory, or animal misery—it naturally leaves this world for another.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00323

When the soul leaves the body, death occurs. This is the natural term of life referred to in scripture: “Every soul will taste death.” It is different from sudden death caused by chance events or forced disruptions. In general, death is natural for the body: the soul parts from it by nature and stops using it because its life has reached a new, fuller state. It may become happy, joyful, and content in itself, like the angels; miserable, consumed by the fire of God that reaches the heart, like devils and evildoers; or forgiven, cleansed of its inner aims and veils. Other animal souls are consumed by the fires of nature for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except those God wills to save from suffering and punishment.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00324

The world is like a farm, and women's wombs are like fields. “Your women are a field for you.” Semen in the wombs is like seed in a field; birth is like a plant emerging; the days of youth are like growth; middle age is like ripening; and old age is like drying. After these stages comes the harvest: death. The grave and the path are like the threshing floor.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00325

On the threshing floor, crops of every kind are gathered, trodden, and sifted. The husks, straw, and leaves are separated from the fruit and grain; some are made fodder for animals or fuel for fires, while some are kept as sound grain. In the same way, all peoples, from the first to the last, will be gathered in the afterlife: “The first and the last will all be brought together at the appointed time of a known day.” Secrets will be laid bare, and God will separate what is vile from what is good. He will pile the vile together and cast it into Hell; He will rescue those who were mindful of Him, so that no harm will touch them and they will not grieve. All this is drawn from several passages in God's noble Book.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00326

The Prophet also said, “This world is the field of the next.” This is the wisdom of death, shown by proof and by the Qur'an. Death is a mercy from God to His friends and a gift to the believer. That is why God's friends long for death. God rebukes those who falsely claim to be among them: “Say: ‘You who are Jews, if you claim that you alone are God's friends, apart from all other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.’”
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00327

Human souls, and other souls too, naturally long for death. They are like craftsmen, while bodies and limbs are like workshops, and the body's powers are like tools. A craftsman works in a workshop for a purpose. When the work is complete and he has reached his aim, he leaves the workshop, sets down his tools, and rests. Likewise, when souls have completed what was required of them in union with the body, and each has developed its capacities in the way it was made to, they turn to themselves. The body then becomes a burden and keeps them from returning to their own homes and sources. Souls have their own sources, like mines of gold and silver, as the hadith says. Death, then, is wisdom and mercy from God, as He says: “Then He causes you to die, then gives you life; then to Him you will return.” The father of the prophets, Abraham, peace be upon him, said: “He is the One who causes me to die, then brings me to life.”
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00328
VII. What We Need to Know About the Formative Power
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00329

Let us first present what has been said about this power, then explain what we take to be true. One of the leading later philosophers says: “In my view, the formative power is unreal, because these actions cannot come from a power that has no awareness.” We have already explained how powers are aware of themselves and of what they do. Another thinker before him said that these actions, and similar ones usually assigned to plant powers, come from angels. Once you understand the kinds of angels God has and how they act by His permission, you will see that the highest ranks are too exalted to carry out such lowly actions directly, without the help of servants and assistants. We have also shown that powers which directly perform changing physical actions must themselves be bodily, while the powers that understand truths applying to many things, wise purposes, and general benefits exist apart from bodies. So the question returns to the powers that act directly: how do they form and shape things? Most theologians, such as the Ashʿarites, assign all these acts to God alone, without a mediator or a specific cause, since they allow an act to be preferred by the will without any reason for that choice. You have already seen the problem with this view.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00330

Others, such as the Muʿtazilites, say that one act produces another. This, too, conflicts with the unity of all action under God. Here is the real difficulty. It seems impossible that the formative power could produce the organs—their shapes, sizes, positions, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness—because semen is uniform in its parts. The power in it must spread through every part. But one power working on one uniform material can produce only one uniform effect. The shape it produces should therefore be a sphere. If there is one formative power in the animal, the whole animal should be one sphere. If there are several powers, each acting on a different part of the uniform material, the animal should be a collection of spheres. This objection has been strengthened by the following disagreement.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00331

Aristotle and his followers say that semen is uniform in all its parts because it comes only from the testes, not from the whole body: each small portion of it has the same name and definition as the whole. Hippocrates and his followers say that semen is not uniform. They say it comes from the whole body: from flesh comes something like flesh, from bone something like bone, and so on for every part. On this account, the organs in semen are unlike one another because they come from organs that differ in kind. They are also unlike the whole, as is plain if this account is accepted. The whole would not be uniform throughout, but would be a mixture of different parts that the senses cannot distinguish, though they remain distinct in reality.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00332

Explaining the animal's different organs by saying that the parts of semen differ does not help solve the problem. It brings back the very difficulty this view was meant to avoid, and adds another impossibility: that semen is already a complete animal with all its organs. If the parts of semen differ because they come from different organs, and those organs differ because their parts differ, then the difference among the animal's organs is explained by the difference among the animal's organs. This leads either to circular reasoning or to an endless chain of causes. Both are impossible.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00333

Know that it is a poor argument to explain different shapes and forms by matter alone, or by the material part of a thing. Matter is indeterminate in every case. It has no substance of its own apart from the form it receives. So saying that the semen causes the different shapes of an animal's organs is just as impossible as saying that matter, considered before it has any particular form, causes all the different forms in the world. Matter in that state can only receive forms; it cannot make something actual, single it out, or make it necessary.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00334

Some people have tried to prove that semen is not uniform by using the same arguments as Hippocrates and his followers, as Avicenna reports in the eleventh chapter of the eleventh treatise of The Healing. He says they relied on three points. First, pleasure is felt throughout the body during ejaculation; if semen did not come from the whole body, the pleasure would be confined to the organ from which it came. Second, resemblance between parent and child is general: if every organ did not send a portion, the child would resemble the parent only in one organ. Third, a child sometimes resembles a parent in a damaged or unusual organ, or has an extra part. They say that if semen is made of different kinds of matter, what comes from flesh forms flesh, and what comes from bone forms bone. The animal should not have to be a sphere.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00335

There are three answers. First, as we have already indicated, this brings back circular reasoning or an endless chain of causes. Second, as we have also said, matter is what a thing can become. In itself it is indeterminate and unclear; it only becomes actual through something that singles it out. The question is precisely what causes the animal's matter to take on the different forms of its organs. Saying that the parts of semen differ does not answer this. If we suppose that semen is made of different parts, we must still ask what caused them to differ. And any compound made of unlike parts must contain simple parts that are alike. Each of these parts must have one simple power working on simple matter. Such a power can produce only one uniform effect. It must therefore produce a sphere, so that the animal formed from semen would be several spheres joined together.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00336

Third, Aristotle questioned whether these arguments are sound and whether semen really comes from all the organs. He gave ten arguments for his view in The Healing; they are also quoted in the commentary on the general parts of The Canon. First, a child can resemble a parent in the nails, though no semen comes from the nails. Second, a child may resemble a distant ancestor, though no seed from that ancestor remains in the family. It is said that a dark-skinned woman gave birth to a white girl, who later gave birth to a dark-skinned child.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00337

Third, semen is not sent out by the body's compound organs as organs, even though it is those organs that resemble one another. Fourth, if semen were as described, it would already be an animal, because it would contain part of every organ. If these parts were arranged in their proper places, semen would be a tiny human being. If they were not arranged, what arranged them?
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00338

Fifth, if a woman releases semen when the man does, then two kinds of semen enter the womb; that would mean two human beings are formed there. Sixth, if a woman's semen already contained separately formed organs, what would prevent her from conceiving when she released semen without a man? The answer to this point also answers the fifth. Seventh, a person may first have male children and later have female children. This is due to a change in temperament, not because the semen once carried male organs and later carried female organs. If temperament can account for the difference between male and female, it can account for other bodily differences too, without the parts being transferred from each organ.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00339

Eighth, many animals are produced from a different species. Ninth, one mating may produce several young, sometimes both male and female. Tenth, a branch taken from a tree that has not yet borne fruit can be planted and later bear fruit. It should not be able to do so if it came from a tree that had not borne fruit and if every part of the branch were already a matching part of that tree's fruit. The supporters of the mixture theory might answer that the parts of the future fruit are mixed into the branch. If so, the same could be true of animals. One would not need seed from every part of the body; a single part would suffice, since it contains all the parts.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00340

These arguments show that resemblance is not caused by different forms in the material. It comes from the formative power, which works according to the readiness of the material prepared by the changing power. These are the arguments Avicenna reports from Aristotle for the view that semen is uniform in its parts. There is room to question most of them, as the commentator al-Shirazi does in his commentary on the general parts. Perhaps Aristotle did not mean them as proofs. He may have wanted to answer the arguments for semen being unlike in its parts with other arguments based on the same kinds of evidence, supporting the view that it is uniform.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00341

I say that the truth, established by proof, goes further than Aristotle's view. Semen is not, by itself, a fully formed substance of its own kind, like a mineral or another complete natural substance. It cannot remain as it is for even an hour, as other waste fluids can. Its condition is like that of first matter: its substance is incomplete until forms are added to it, and through them it becomes a particular kind of thing and is changed into that thing.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00342

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi argues in The Investigations that semen has different parts. He says it is the waste product of the last stage of digestion. That stage occurs when the blood has matured and is fully ready to become the substance of the organs. This is why losing semen weakens a person more than losing ten times as much blood: it draws on the original substances of the organs. If so, semen must consist of parts, each close to becoming a particular organ. This would mean its mixture is uniform, but its parts are not.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00343

This argument, too, is weak for several reasons. First, as you have learned, the food that actually nourishes an animal is not the food that enters the body from outside, nor is it the food that has merely changed through digestion. In truth, an animal is nourished by what comes from within itself and is strengthened by its own inner power. What people call foods and medicines are only things that prepare the body's matter to be acted on by its own source, in a way suited to it. This is like the difference between what is potentially understood and what is actually understood. What is called potentially understood never becomes an actual object of thought on its own; it only prepares the soul to become actually thinking and to have something actually understood. Likewise, flesh and bone do not become what they are simply because food has entered the body.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00344

A ligament, too, becomes a ligament according to the soul's patterns, qualities, parts, and powers. These forms pass from the world of spiritual meanings into the world of bodily shapes through the movements and changes that prepare the food and other matter.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00345
Second, even if semen is the product of the fourth digestion, why must waste be the same as, or close to, what it replaces? Is animal dung like the animal? Is human sweat like a human being?
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00346

Third, suppose semen, while still joined to the organ-forming power, was like the organs or nearly ready to become them. Once it leaves those organs and moves to another place, we cannot assume it keeps the same arrangement. What preserves its parts in their order, position, and quality? If the parents' souls preserve them, how can one soul naturally govern and preserve more than one body? A soul does not act throughout any body other than its own. If it acted in the semen, the semen would no longer be semen; it would be an animal with a soul. Nor does weakness after ejaculation show that semen has different parts. The weakness has a psychic cause: bodily pleasure affects the soul, and the resulting weakness spreads through the body, as fear and other states of the soul can disturb it and weaken its powers and main organs. In short, semen is matter that can receive the organs. A thing that can receive something must be free of that thing and its opposite; otherwise it would already have what it is meant to receive, or it would contain opposites at once. Both are impossible.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00347

Semen is also a flowing moisture. Such a fluid cannot contain different arrangements and qualities in separate parts, clearly enough to make it a means for producing different forms and effects. We have already seen that differences in readiness and lack of readiness are possibilities and relations; they do not exist on their own, but only depend on other things.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00348

Before we prove that plants and animals have a formative power, you must understand one more point. What we ascribe to matter and its readiness can only concern particular details: specific times, places, and positions. But regular features shared by every member of a kind must come from causes capable of producing them across that whole kind.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00349

With that established, we can see that the different shapes, structures, sizes, and positions of organs—and the particular shape each organ has for the benefit of human beings and animals—cannot be explained by the material of semen, for the reasons already given. This is especially clear in the organs of the head: the eye and its layers, nose, mouth, teeth, tongue, lips, and all their uses. Some are needed for survival; others bring ease, excellence, or beauty, such as eyelashes, dark eyebrows, and the arch of the foot.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00350

Nor can these features come from a lower power such as bodily nature. Nature acts in one pattern, toward one or at most two ends. It cannot account for the many purposes, motives, and aims found in a body. These forms must come from powers of the soul, guided by higher purposes that lead to the world of intellect and the divine mystery.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00351

Let us put the whole question in general terms. The active cause of an animal's body must be either something without knowledge or awareness, such as bodily nature and similar powers, or something that has knowledge and awareness. The first option is impossible: every sound human nature knows that the maker of this wonderful order and firm arrangement cannot be a power with no awareness. The second option is either God acting directly, without a mediator, or some other cause.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00352

The first is impossible, as shown by decisive arguments and by revealed teachings. God's essence is too exalted to perform particular, changing, perishable acts. Anyone who attributes such changes and actions to Him has not understood the Lord's true nature or what it means to be divine; they have not given God the reverence due to Him. They have also misunderstood what it means to act and cause. Every effect exists through its nearest cause, as light exists through what gives light and speech through a speaker—not as a building exists through a builder.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00353

Anyone deeply versed in knowledge of God, which reaches beyond the study of physical nature, knows that all beings come from God, without time or place, through powers, souls, and natural processes that He has set to work. God gives life, causes death, provides for creation, guides some and misleads others. But the angel who directly brings life is named Israfil; the angel who brings death is named Azrael, taking souls from bodies, bodies from food, and food from the earth. The angel who provides sustenance is Mika'il, who knows the measure and amount of food. The angel of guidance is Gabriel. The agent of misguidance is not an angel but a devilish being named Azazil. Each of these angels has helpers and hosts of powers placed under God's command, as do His other acts. If God were the direct agent of every lowly act, He would have created the means that carry out His commands without purpose. Exalted is He above creating anything useless or leaving it inactive; this is what those who deny Him suppose.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00354

If the cause is not God acting directly, it must be either a being that knows and exists without matter—one of the higher intellects or exalted angels—or a soul. The first is impossible for the reason already given: their actions do not change or multiply into separate instances across time. These beings are not separate in their essence from the First Reality. They are rays of His sun and lights of His light; their being is lost in His being, and their lights are gathered into His light.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00355

As for the soul as the cause of the body, it either acts by choice, after a purpose, will, and knowledge beyond its own being, or it does not. The first is false. Even now, with all our knowledge, we do not know the shapes, sizes, positions, and structures of our organs until we study anatomy. How could we have known and chosen these things at the very beginning of our existence? It remains that the soul is the cause of the body and its organs. But the soul either acts independently or in obedience to a command from God and His unseen realm, as a servant. It cannot act independently, because it does not exist independently. How much less could it create? When the organs are taking shape and their forms are first appearing, the human soul is at its weakest and least developed. At that time, a person has no control over their own benefit or harm, life or death, or resurrection.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00356

The cause that shapes these bodies, organs, and arrangements must be a wise maker and an all-knowing guide. So the only possibility left is that the one who creates, shapes, and forms these bodies, nourishes and grows them, and brings them forth is a command from God, using the soul and its powers in obedience to God's will and wisdom. By God's command, the soul passes through different stages. At one stage, as in the womb, it gives suitable forms to matter and bodies. At another, it gives the powers of sensation forms that suit the senses and the things they sense, carrying images of the world of light into the world of darkness. At another stage, it gives inner powers images of imagination and thought.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00357

At a later stage, the soul gives beings the forms of divine truths, meanings, and knowledge. This is how we should understand the account of some wise philosophers about how an embryo forms. Matter is prepared for one thing: the soul. But the soul has different organs, needs, and powers that are joined in a certain way. The matter must therefore have different potential capacities, which unite in a special way: through the body's temperament.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00358

The powers that arise in it must also have structures that allow them to act. Through these structures, one organ divides into many; the different arrangements of the powers produce the different positions of the organs. It is like the way what comes after the first intellect and active intellect comes from the forms and patterns already present in them. Just as these forms are present in the intellects, the shape of a human being is present in the nutritive power, with the help of matter. This is how the philosopher explains it.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00359

His purpose is to show that these acts can come from the soul through its powers and states, without being impossible or surprising. Every being whose existence proceeds from God, who depends on nothing else contains, within its unity, many qualities, states, and meanings suited to its level and rank. In this, it reflects the First Cause: one, yet containing all divine qualities and names. You have already learned that God is all things without being many. The closer a being is to Him, the more unified it is and the more meanings it gathers. Each being is, in itself, a world that reflects the world of Lordship.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00360

The human soul gathers within itself all the powers and organs that are spread throughout the body. The different shapes of the organs are shadows of the different powers of perception and movement spread through them, just as the spirit that comes from the heart spreads through the veins and arteries. Though these powers differ and branch out, they are gathered in the soul and joined with it, as the intellect is joined with what it understands.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00361

In short, lower powers branch out and spread when they flow from higher powers. They then act in different ways to serve the purposes of the powers above them, even if they do not know those purposes. The powers that draw, digest, and expel food act for the soul's purposes as it governs the body, though the powers of drawing and digestion do not know those purposes on their own. They act by following and serving the soul.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00362

The same is true of powers of perception. Hearing and sight serve the soul, and what they perceive is the soul's own perception. The soul itself has hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch. That is why it can perceive these things in dreams when the outer senses are inactive. Each sense, when it acts, serves the soul by its very nature. The formative power works in the same way.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00363
It shapes the organs according to the soul's purposes, needs, and aims.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00364

No one should object that the formative power is bodily and has no awareness of these aims, and ask how it can produce actions that serve them, as though it had been created for these benefits and goals. The answer is that a higher power—the soul—uses it. Someone may reply: “But we know that our souls are not aware of these purposes, benefits, and advantages.”
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00365

We answer: while your soul’s abilities are still undeveloped, it is like the formative power, which acts directly in service to a power above it. If your soul developed those abilities fully, the light of insight would show you that it uses all the other powers, its own soldiers and servants, for wise purposes and benefits that protect the individual or the kind, whether in this life or another. When the philosopher said that matter is prepared for one thing, the soul, he meant that matter is semen and that its readiness is remote. Through many changes, this readiness can gradually become near. The only thing that first flows into it from the soul is a form that preserves its structure from decay. But this form can grow stronger and more complete until it reaches a higher level. The same is true at each level.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00366

The philosopher's claim that the soul has different organs, needs, and powers joined in a certain way refers to the soul's different levels and stations. Everything that becomes one of the soul's powers or instruments acts before the user of that power comes into being. Its action prepares it to receive the flow of another form, which will use and rule it, without rebellion. This continues through every stage of the soul. Each power is made by nature to act in a way that does not oppose the aim of what is above it, but moves toward that aim and follows its path.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00367

This answers the objection that, if the formative power belongs to the soul, the instrument would act before the user—the soul—came into being. Before the soul flows into it, the power is not yet an instrument of the soul. It is a form or first completion, like other animal or plant powers that arise before the human soul. When the animal form, or even the earlier plant form, appears in the body's matter, there is no doubt that it acts on its own, as a ruler, not as an instrument.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00368

Later, as it becomes more complete and its being grows stronger, it reaches the rational level and joins with it. Its own being then becomes subject to, and obedient to, the command of God. It performs the same actions it performed before, now in service to this higher being. This is what it means for the powers to be joined in a certain way. The human soul itself understands general kinds and individual things, senses and moves, nourishes, grows, reproduces, and keeps the body's temperament. In short, it itself does all that the inanimate form, plant soul, and animal soul did. By being one, it is all these substances, each of which exists outside it as a separate, complete kind.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00369

When the philosopher says that matter has different potential capacities that unite with it in a certain way—namely, the body's temperament—he does not mean that semen is ready from the beginning for all the powers, organs, and features of the soul. Someone might object that a seed cannot receive the rational soul and its powers until it has become a human body, but it cannot become a human body until those powers and organs already exist. As we have explained many times, near readiness always follows from forms and qualities that already exist. What makes a thing ready is not the readiness itself, nor is it the thing that can be received. It must be suited to what it is ready for and lie on the path toward it, as each earlier stage in a movement prepares the next.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00370

The philosopher means that semen is a substance which, through a series of changes, can receive successive stages of readiness. These changes end in a human body with different organs, all connected to one organ, the heart, whose relation to the other organs is like the soul's relation to its powers. The readinesses that exist as many and varied powers in the heart and organs all began, while still potential, from one readiness that could receive and give rise to them. This is the temperament of semen. It must be balanced: no one side of its qualities should dominate, and no quality should be fully active at the expense of another. Then it can receive a complete form that gives rise to all the opposing powers—attraction and repulsion, desire and anger, love and dislike, and actions that belong to nature, sensation, or reason. If the matter already had one of these natures or forms in actuality, it could not receive them all. That is why human semen is so weak in its own substance.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00371

When the philosopher says that what came after the first intellect and the active intellect was already present in them, he means that each active power contains, in its complete unity, the realities that flow from it later in detail—just as the sea contains raindrops and a mountain contains small stones. When he says that the shapes are “imprinted” in the intellects, and so the shape of a human being is “imprinted” in the nutritive power, with the help of matter, he does not mean that the organs are already pictured inside that power. Philosophers agree that it has no awareness. Even the soul, which is stronger, does not know the organs' shapes and arrangements until it studies anatomy. He means that the power contains aspects and directions suited to those shapes, because it serves as an intermediary in the flow of forms from their higher sources.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00372

Do not think that we mean God or the active intellects are places in which forms grasped by the mind are pictured. Our view, which some ancient philosophers also held, is that each actual knower is joined with what it knows. We have explained this carefully, leaving no room for doubt. Every higher power therefore contains whatever is below it in a more complete and simpler way. Philosophers agree that the creator of all is one being, wholly simple and perfectly one. Yet they also agree that this one being creates bodies and animal organs. See what they say about divine providence, and read Galen's On the Use of the Parts, as well as the works of Hippocrates, Plato, and others on anatomy. They all agree that God creates bodies and organs. This does not prevent them from accepting intellectual intermediaries, powers of the soul, and natural instruments, each acting according to God's decree. A wise person does not personally sweep, carry away waste, or work in a rubbish heap. Their own work is to judge, command, guide, decree, send down, and send forth—not to perform every movement and bodily change. Anyone who denies that the intermediaries act according to their nature has not understood God's greatness, as scripture says: “They have not measured God with the measure He deserves,” when they say, “God has sent nothing down to any human being.”
